transcript: So I don't know for a fact that Heathers isn't going to Broadway, but here's why I feel comfortable saying it very likely won't. So this revival of Heathers the musical currently playing off Broadway is a commercial, for-profit production And from what I can tell, it's functionally an open ended run? They do call their new block of tickets an “extension,” which is an increasingly common marketing tactic. I don't think they actually intend to close as long as ticket sales hold out. In either case, the context clues here are telling us that Broadway is probably not their goal. The general rule of thumb, at least from what I've observed, is that if a show is playing a commercial off-Broadway run, it's probably because that's where they ended up deciding to be instead of Broadway. Sure, off-Broadway shows transferred to Broadway all the time, but usually from a limited run at a non-profit theatre. Sometimes we get comedy shows and like special event entertainment productions that go from a commercial off-Broadway run to Broadway, but for traditional plays and musicals it's pretty rare. Commercial Broadway and commercial off-Broadway are essentially uppercase and lowercase versions of the same letter; They're roughly the same model, just on a different scale. So producers usually pick a lane between them based on which one is more attainable and commercially viable. Now to be fair, we did have two exceptions to this quite recently, both Job and Oh Mary played commercial runs off Broadway before transferring to Broadway. It was very unusual, though. I was surprised that it even happened once, let alone twice at the same time. Before that, I think the last time it happened with a play or musical was Be More Chill  in 2018. But what these three shows all had in common is, in their own way, they were *surprise* runaway hits. Even the venues they chose off-Broadway couldn't accommodate long open runs. Meanwhile, Job and Be More Chill didn't do that well on Broadway. They sort of overestimated how much demand would translate, further demonstrating why people rarely take the risk. Oh Mary, on the other hand, has proven to be the genuine once in a blue moon exception. But unlike any of those shows, Heather's is a long-established IP With a long-established target audience. So when producers decided to take this from London to New York, they had a clear, calculated assessment of which path was right for them. And they chose off Broadway. The demand was never gonna wildly exceed their expectations, as it would have to, by a very wide margin, to make it worth jeopardizing what's already working for them. Even if ticket sales were a lot better than they hoped, it's still a lot easier, safer, and smarter to react by just continuing to run longer off Broadway.
